title: Title I built a free Tools/Index that shows the odds of breaking the prior high, the odds of going higher, and how hard runners are getting dumped
author: eyeneedtoblink1
selftext:
I went through the last year and a half and kept only the runners that went up 30% or more. I turned how those names actually moved into probabilities. One number is the chance a stock breaks its prior high before the regular session ends. The other is the chance it goes beyond that, into the next zone.

I also built the Dump Index. It measures how far runners fell, and how fast. Zero means they are holding up. The farther below zero it goes, the more today's 30%+ runners have dropped, and the faster they did it. The number only means something next to yesterday, the 5-day average, and the 20-day average. That is how you judge how heavy the dump is.

The plain Dump Index has a flaw. It is the average score of every name already in it. As the day goes on and more names get added, a new runner moves that average less and less. The new names get buried under the old ones. That is why I made the current-reaction dump index. It shows the dump on the names that are showing up now.

Here is how I read them.

If the current-reaction dump index and the plain Dump Index are not far apart, the dump has been going on all day, and it is still going on. When a new runner shows up, scalp it in seconds. Do not get greedy.

Runners also have a clear habit. They come out in a bunch, then it goes quiet, then they come out in a bunch again. I call that quiet stretch no-man's-land. In no-man's-land the current-reaction dump gets light, closer to zero, while the plain Dump Index can still be deep in the red from earlier. So if the current-reaction dump is light and the Dump Index is still heavy, I read it as no-man's-land, or as the start of new runners coming out. An uptrend.

The Dump Index is hard to use. That part is fair, and it still needs a lot of work. People who learn it will probably get a lot out of it. Beginners will probably find it confusing. I am working on a simpler reading, closer to a fear-and-greed gauge. I expect that within about two weeks, after a math professor checks the math.

I did not build this site to make money. Everything on it is free. I just want people to stop losing money they cannot afford on runners. That is the whole point.

Warren Buffett's first rule is never lose money. May it be with you, like the Force.

https://www.whyup.net/similar-movers

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Saying plainly that the Dump Index is hard to read and getting the math checked is the right instinct. The numbers I'd want next to the probabilities are how many past runners each percentage is based on (a 71.2% from 40 stocks is very different from one from 4,000), and how it did on a stretch it wasn't built from, because probabilities fitted on the last year and a half will look better on that same period. Also check what counts as the "prior high" when a stock gaps up in pre-market, and whether the list of names is filtered after the fact, since keeping only the runners that went up 30% leaves out the ones that never got there, which can flatter the odds. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to see how rules get compared against a benchmark.

replies.author: eyeneedtoblink1
replies.body:
First of all, I am thrilled to finally talk with someone who has put serious thought into this. It honestly feels like escaping a deserted island! If you read this till the end, you will see the direction of my research.

Let me address the sample size first. I am well aware that a small sample size can just be random noise, so I am actively trying to prevent that. Up to around the 300% high mark, the sample size ranges from at least 1,000 to as many as 50,000 cases. The problem is beyond that point—the sample size gets way too small. Naturally, excluding warrants and preferred stocks, there just aren't that many common stocks that run over 300%. 

At first glance, the solution seems simple: "Why not just extend the lookback period way beyond 1.5 years?" However, there is a hidden trap here. 

The ecosystem of momentum runners is truly fascinating. It operates almost independently from the broader stock market. In this space, yesterday's theme influences today, and today influences tomorrow. The catch is that this influence dilutes over time—much like genetics. As time passes and generations go by, relatives eventually become strangers. Metaphorically speaking, a week is like an immediate family, a quarter is a clan, and a year is an entire ethnic group. This transition isn't abrupt; it happens gradually. 

You probably see where I'm going with this. Once you go past 1.5 years, you are essentially comparing two completely different ethnic groups (market regimes). 

Also, I didn't curve-fit a strategy to generate profit. I simply gathered raw statistics using very basic conditions and expressed them as conditional probabilities without arbitrary filtering. Every single day, my model updates these probabilities using a rolling window—dropping the oldest day from the 1.5-year period and adding the newest day. That way, as time goes on, the statistics always remain a description of the "same ethnic group." And of course, I am not claiming this is an absolute law; it is simply a probabilistic representation of observed behaviors.

I'm not sure if I've articulated my fragmented thoughts logically here. I'm just an ordinary student, so it's only natural for me to be wrong about things. If you can explain your points logically and in detail so that I can be convinced (though I might be too slow to grasp it right away!), I am all ears. Thank you so much for the feedback!

replies.author: eyeneedtoblink1
replies.body: Oh, I forgot to mention this—because the sample size for the >300% range is so small, I am currently working on finding a proper solution for it.

replies.author: eyeneedtoblink1
replies.body: One more thing—I genuinely don't know much about where to find communities for this, so if you know any places where people passionately debate this kind of stuff, please let me know! I really want to learn more.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: laces to talk about this kind of thing: r/algotrading and r/quant for the statistics side, r/Daytrading for how people actually use runner and momentum data, and r/pinescript if you want to share the logic as an indicator. Each has its own self-promotion rules, so read them before posting a link.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: For the 300%+ bucket, the sample is small by nature, so I’d either merge it with the nearest bucket and say so, or show a range (a confidence interval) instead of a single number. A range like “between 15% and 45%” is more honest than “28%” when there are only a few dozen cases behind it.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That’s a good reason for the rolling window, and the “same ethnic group” idea is clear to me: you want the statistics to describe the current regime and not an average of different ones. The cost is that the window gets short for the rare cases, so it would help to show the count behind every percentage on the page and grey out any bucket below a minimum (say 30 cases), so a reader can’t mistake a thin number for a firm one.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: depends when the 30% gets measured. if a name qualifies by its high of the day, every stock that touched 28% and faded never makes the set, so the break-the-high odds come out better than what you'd actually see at 10am.

replies.author: eyeneedtoblink1
replies.body:
To clarify how the data is collected: a stock qualifies and enters the dataset the exact moment it crosses the 30% threshold intraday, not retroactively based on the end-of-day high. 

The reason I set 30% as the trigger point comes down to the specific ecosystem I am studying—mostly micro-caps and penny stocks with very thin order books. Because of their low float and high volatility, by the time these stocks show up on the radar of ordinary retail traders (who just look at standard "Top Gainers" lists rather than professional real-time scanners), they are already up well over 30%. 

So my model isn't trying to predict the odds of a 28% stock breaking 30%. Instead, crossing the 30% mark is the baseline trigger event where retail FOMO actually begins, and the probabilities track what happens from that exact moment onward. Because it is measured from the moment the 30% threshold is crossed, there is no look-ahead bias from filtering by the end-of-day high.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that matters a lot, thanks. if a stock enters at the moment it crosses 30%, measure what happens next from the cross price, not that day's open or close. otherwise a name that tagged 30% and faded to 8% by the bell looks the same as one that closed at 45%.

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
Odds like these get questioned fast in trading subs, so the first comments will likely ask how you define a runner, what counts as getting dumped, and which tickers and date range the odds come from. Since this went up as a gallery with no text, a first comment with those three definitions and one worked ticker example would answer that before it starts, and makes the index easier to trust when you share it elsewhere.
